title: Μυῖαι
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 239 (= Perry 80). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔν τινι ταμιείῳ μέλιτος ἐπεκχυθέντος, μυῖαι προσπτᾶσαι κατήσθιον· διὰ δὲ τὴν γλυκύτητα τοῦ καρποῦ οὐκ ἀφίσταντο.
sentences.tr: En tini tamieiōi melitos epekchythentos, muiai prosptasai katēsthion· dia de tēn glykytēta tou karpou ouk aphistanto.
sentences.l: In a certain storeroom, honey having been spilled out, flies, having flown to it, were devouring it; and because of the sweetness of the yield they would not stand off.
sentences.i: Honey had been spilled in a storeroom, and flies flew to it and set about devouring it; and because the stuff was so sweet they would not leave off.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (μέλιτος ἐπεκχυθέντος) sets the scene before the flies arrive — Greek's regular way of laying down a circumstance that has a subject of its own. καρπός is properly the fruit or yield of anything, and honey is the bees' crop. Both imperfects (κατήσθιον, ἀφίσταντο) keep the flies at it: they went on eating, they kept not standing off.

sentences.t: Ἐμπαγέντων δὲ αὐτῶν τῶν ποδῶν, ὡς οὐκ ἐδύναντο ἀναπτῆναι, ἀποπνιγόμεναι ἔφασαν· « Ἄθλιαι ἡμεῖς, αἳ διὰ βραχεῖαν ἡδονὴν ἀπολλύμεθα. »
sentences.tr: Empagentōn de autōn tōn podōn, hōs ouk edynanto anaptēnai, apopnigomenai ephasan· « Athliai hēmeis, hai dia bracheian hēdonēn apollymetha. »
sentences.l: But their feet having been fixed fast, since they could not fly up, being choked they said: « Wretched we, who for a brief pleasure are perishing. »
sentences.i: But their feet stuck fast, and since they could not fly up, they said as they drowned: « Wretched creatures that we are, perishing for a moment's pleasure. »
sentences.n: ἐμπαγέντων is the aorist passive participle of ἐμπήγνυμι, 'fix in', in a second genitive absolute; the possessive genitive αὐτῶν stands outside the article group (αὐτῶν τῶν ποδῶν, 'the feet of them'), which is the regular place for the genitive of αὐτός. ὡς here is causal, 'since'. ἀπόλλυμαι in the middle is intransitive, 'perish' — no one is destroying them but themselves. Ἄθλιαι ἡμεῖς has no verb: ἐσμέν is simply left out, as Greek regularly leaves out the copula.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοῖς ἡ λιχνεία πολλῶν αἰτία κακῶν γίνεται.
sentences.tr: Houtō pollois hē lichneia pollōn aitia kakōn ginetai.
sentences.l: So for many gluttony becomes a cause of many evils.
sentences.n: λιχνεία is greed at the table in particular — daintiness, the licking after sweet things — which is exactly the flies' fault and not some general vice. The jingle of πολλοῖς … πολλῶν holds the sentence together in Greek and can only be half kept in English.
